newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania to ban pyramid schemes as protests go on.
newsitem.headline: Albania to ban pyramid schemes as protests go on.

text.p: Albanians, some left penniless after the collapse of pyramid investment schemes, protested in the Adriatic port of Durres on Thursday as parliament assembled to consider banning the dubious investment funds outright.

Around 2,000 demonstrators, accompanied by senior members of the opposition Socialist Party, attempted to converge on the main square of Durres, 40 km (25 miles) west of Tirana, but were stopped by police, witnesses said.
"You have to understand us because we are of the people like you, but we have our orders," one police officer was heard telling the protesters. There were no reports of clashes or violence.
The financial scandals have stirred up the opposition to try to make political capital out of the anger among investors against the ruling right-wing Democratic Party.
The Durres protest was staged as the government of President Sali Berisha tabled a draft law in parliament to ban pyramid schemes and offer compensation to depositors.
"The council of ministers tabled the draft law on the prohibition of the pyramid schemes...to protect the interests of individuals from exploitation," state news agency ATA said.
The government also intended to get tough with pyramid scheme operators and could propose up to 20 years in jail for the main operators and more than 10 years for associates.
Albania could prohibit the pyramid schemes, which have proliferated since the fall of communism in 1990, at a stroke.
But compensating thousands of investors who have poured millions of dollars into the schemes will not be easy for a government struggling to cut a big budget deficit.
Albania's central bank figures put the budget deficit last October at 23.9 billion leks (around $240 million), the equivalent of about 10 percent of gross domestic product.
Authorities have seized around 25.5 billion leks ($255 million) deposited by two collapsed schemes in state-owned banks but the figure may not be enough to quell the anger of Albanians who face ruin.
Protests have spread as investors in Europe's poorest nation faced losing their life savings, some after selling their homes, flocks of sheep and cows and other belongings.
Thousands clashed with baton-wielding police in Tirana on Sunday in a demonstration against the schemes, the biggest of several protests around Albania over the past two weeks.
More than 50 people were jailed or given big fines for taking part in Sunday's protest, described by the authorities as an illegal demonstration.
Hundreds demonstrated in the northern city of Shkoder on Thursday, calling for the government's resignation.
"The government should resign, we want our money," protesters shouted.
Shkoder mayor Bahri Borici told the crowd he sympathised with their plight as he too had invested in the schemes.
"I live with your concern but I think such problems should be resolved calmly," he told the demonstrators.
